title: Carryforward of ITC - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Find out how the 20-year Carryforward of ITC lets you save unused R&D tax credits for future years in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: In Canada, unused SR&ED investment tax credits (ITCs) that exceed federal Part I tax payable and are not refunded in cash can be carried forward up to 20 taxation years or carried back up to 3 years. This applies to SR&ED claimants under the Income Tax Act; any portion applied against tax payable or refunded in cash reduces the balance.

body.text: In Canada, unused SR&ED investment tax credits (ITCs) that exceed federal Part I tax payable and are not refunded in cash can be carried forward up to 20 taxation years or carried back up to 3 years. This applies to SR&ED claimants under the Income Tax Act; any portion applied against tax payable or refunded in cash reduces the balance.

Between late 2024 and November 2026, Canada enacted the most expansive structural overhaul of its flagship Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program in over a decade, rendering pre-2026 tax summaries materially outdated. Specifically, Bill C-15—which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacting the legislative reforms from Federal Budget 2025—doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (superseding the $4.5 million interim proposal in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and reinstated SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures and shared-use equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024. Administratively, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026 featuring an eight-week determination standard and issued revised SR&ED tax forms in May 2026. Most recently, Federal Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) proposed an additional $930 million five-year SR&ED expansion alongside a $36 billion Productivity Mega Deduction, while Québec abolished eight legacy innovation tax measures in favour of its unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025.
1. Statutory Architecture and 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms
1.1 Core Statutory Framework Under the Income Tax Act and Regulations

Canada's federal R&D tax incentive architecture is codified in the Income Tax Act (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), with tax policy formulated by the Department of Finance Canada and claims administered by the Canada Revenue Agency. Rather than relying on an income super-deduction, the federal SR&ED program delivers fiscal support through a two-pronged statutory mechanism. First, under section 37 of the ITA, taxpayers carrying on business in Canada pool allowable current SR&ED expenditures—and, following the enactment of paragraph 37(1)(b), eligible capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024—to take an immediate 100% deduction against business income in the taxation year incurred or carry unused deductible pool balances forward to offset income in future taxation years. Second, under sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA (specifically subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and 127.1(2.01)), claimants earn an Investment Tax Credit equal to 15% or 35% of their annual "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool," which reduces federal Part I tax payable and, for eligible claimants, yields a partial (40%) or full (100%) cash refund.

The substantive gateway governing technical eligibility for both incentives is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, paired with prescribed proxy calculation and salary-base exclusion rules in section 2900 (including subsections 2900(4), 2900(6), and 2900(9)) of the ITR. From an audit verification standpoint, claimants must distinguish between the multi-year nature of the section 37 income deduction pool and the strictly annual nature of the subsection 127(9) ITC base: while undeducted section 37 expenditures carry over to future years, the "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" is computed strictly at the close of each taxation year to determine that year's ITC entitlement and never carries over as an expenditure pool into a subsequent taxation year.
1.2 Enacted Bill C-15 Reforms (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) vs. Interim 2024 Proposals

Accurate verification of post-2024 Canadian R&D claims requires separating interim policy proposals announced during 2024 and 2025 from the final statutory parameters enacted in 2026. In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement—and in subsequent draft legislative proposals and explanatory notes released by the Department of Finance in August 2025—the federal government initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million. Federal Budget 2025 (tabled November 4, 2025) superseded that interim ceiling by committing an additional $293 million in net federal tax relief over five fiscal years: $3 million in 2025–2026, $70 million in 2026–2027, $85 million in 2027–2028, $65 million in 2028–2029, and $70 million in 2029–2030.

The Budget 2025 SR&ED reforms were enacted into law through Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Applicable retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million, raising the maximum annual enhanced ITC from $1.05 million to $2.10 million. Simultaneously, Bill C-15 broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range for CCPCs from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the 35% enhanced refundable ITC up to the $6 million expenditure limit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a $15 million–$75 million three-year average consolidated revenue phase-out, permitted CCPCs to elect into the ECPC revenue-based limit formula, and restored both section 37 deductions and section 127 ITCs for depreciable capital property and shared-use equipment acquired (and eligible equipment lease costs incurred) after December 15, 2024.
1.3 Federal Budget 2026 Proposals (Tabled November 5, 2026)

On November 5, 2026, the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, tabled Budget 2026 (Masters of Our Destiny) alongside a Notice of Ways and Means Motion to Amend the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations. Under Business Income Tax Measures, Budget 2026 proposes a further expansion of the SR&ED Tax Incentive Program carrying a projected five-year federal revenue impact of $930 million: $25 million in 2026–2027, $200 million in 2027–2028, $245 million in 2028–2029, $225 million in 2029–2030, and $235 million in 2030–2031.

Specifically, Budget 2026 proposes expanding SR&ED eligibility to include tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process, where that work directly relates to an eligible SR&ED project, together with the costs of registering and maintaining intellectual property protection (such as patents, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software) for intellectual property developed in an eligible SR&ED project, excluding enforcement costs such as litigation; the measure would apply to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026. Budget 2026 also introduces two broader business tax measures that directly shape R&D capital deployment and domestic scale-up strategy. First, building on September 15, 2026 draft legislative proposals, the Productivity Mega Deduction provides accelerated capital write-offs—including increasing Canadian development expense deduction rates from 30% to 100% in resource sectors—at an estimated five-year fiscal cost of $36 billion beginning in 2026–2027 to lower effective marginal tax rates on machinery, equipment, and production technology. Second, the Canada Growth Incentive establishes a Capital Gains Exemption and a rollover for small-business investments to retain Canadian innovators, startups, and key employees domestically. Because Budget 2026 proposals had not yet received Royal Assent as of mid-November 2026, auditors must distinguish enacted Bill C-15 law from proposed Budget 2026 expansions.

body.text: 2. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, and Refundability
2.1 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates by Claimant Classification

Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits operate across two statutory rate tiers under section 127 of the ITA. The basic ITC rate of 15% applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by foreign-controlled corporations, public corporations that do not qualify as ECPCs, individuals, sole proprietorships, trusts, and partnerships, as well as to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual expenditure limit. The enhanced ITC rate of 35%—structured under subsection 127(10.1) as an additional 20% credit layered onto the 15% basic credit—applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the annual expenditure limit ($6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) for CCPCs and ECPCs.

Within the corporate sector, refundability and rate rules turn on four distinct statutory classifications. First, a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) (defined in subsection 125(7) of the ITA) is further sub-classified under section 127.1 into: (a) qualifying corporations, meaning CCPCs whose prior-year taxable income (combined with all associated corporations) did not exceed their qualifying income limit for the current year; (b) excluded corporations as defined in subsection 127.1(2), whose refund rate on enhanced current expenditures is restricted to 40%; and (c) other CCPCs (neither qualifying nor excluded), which still receive 100% refundability on the 35% ITC earned on current expenditures up to the expenditure limit pursuant to subsection 127.1(2.01), but earn non-refundable 15% ITCs above the expenditure limit.

Second, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) is a corporation resident in Canada, listed on a designated stock exchange, and not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner by one or more non-resident persons. To prevent fragmented foreign ownership from bypassing control tests, the statute imposes an aggregation rule: even if all shares owned by non-residents were held by a single hypothetical person, an ECPC must still not be controlled by that person. Third, all other corporations—such as Canadian subsidiaries controlled by foreign multinationals or non-qualifying public entities—earn a strictly non-refundable 15% ITC on all qualified expenditures. Fourth, for partnerships, because a partnership is not a separate taxpayer, the 15% ITC is computed at the partnership level in accordance with the SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy and allocated to eligible partners; only partners that are qualifying corporations, individuals, or certain trusts can receive a 40% cash refund of their allocated ITC, whereas other corporate partners receive a non-refundable allocation.
2.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Outs, Consolidated Groups, and Short Tax Years

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 maximum expenditure limit is subject to size-based phase-outs under subsections 127(10.2) through 127(10.64) of the ITA. Under subsection 127(10.2), a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease once its taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year (aggregated across all CCPCs in an associated corporate group) reaches $15,000,000, and is eliminated entirely at $75,000,000. By contrast, for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the legacy $3,000,000 limit began decreasing at $10,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital and reached nil at $50,000,000. Associated CCPCs must file T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) to divide the group's single expenditure limit among associated members.

For ECPCs in taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, new subsection 127(10.6) (together with the application rules in subsections 127(10.61) to 127(10.64)) phases out the $6,000,000 expenditure limit based on average annual revenue rather than taxable capital. Specifically, the limit decreases when average annual revenue over the preceding three fiscal years (or over the actual one or two preceding fiscal years if fewer than three exist) exceeds $15,000,000, becoming nil at $75,000,000. If an ECPC belongs to a consolidated group preparing consolidated financial statements that present group assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows as a single economic entity, the consolidated group's annual revenue governs—even where a subsidiary joins or leaves the group mid-year—and the resulting expenditure limit must be shared across the consolidated members. Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC or group of associated CCPCs may elect under prescribed conditions to disapply the subsection 127(10.2) taxable capital test and instead compute its expenditure limit using the ECPC revenue-based rules, offering substantial relief to equity-rich, pre-revenue or early-revenue Canadian private companies whose balance-sheet capital exceeds $15 million.

Where a corporation has a short taxation year, or where a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC having a taxation year ending in that calendar year, subsection 127(10.5) (renumbered from former subsection 127(10.6) by Bill C-15) prorates the allocated expenditure limit by the number of days in the short taxation year divided by 365. As illustrated in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if an associated CCPC is allocated $3,000,000 of the group limit and experiences a 184-day taxation year running from July 1 to December 31, 2027, its prorated expenditure limit is $3,000,000 × (184 days ÷ 365 days) = $1,512,328.
2.3 Refundability Matrix for Current vs. Capital Expenditures

Under section 127.1 of the ITA, cash refundability of unused SR&ED ITCs (after offsetting current-year Part I tax payable) diverges sharply between current expenditures and reinstated post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures. For CCPCs (other than excluded corporations) and ECPCs, the 35% enhanced ITC earned up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is 100% refundable on current expenditures (delivering a 35.0% cash refund on qualified current spending), whereas the 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit is 40% refundable (delivering an immediate 14.0% cash refund—40% × 35%—with the remaining 21.0% retained as a non-refundable ITC). Above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, qualifying CCPCs and excluded CCPCs continue to receive a 40% cash refund on their 15% ITC (6.0% cash) on both current and capital expenditures, whereas ECPCs and non-qualifying CCPCs receive no cash refund above the expenditure limit.

body.text: 2.4 Carryback, Carryforward, and ITC Recapture Rules

Where earned SR&ED ITCs exceed current-year federal income tax payable and are not refunded in cash, the unused ITC balance may be carried back up to 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset federal Part I tax payable in those years; any portion applied against tax payable or refunded in cash reduces the balance available for carryback or carryforward.

Conversely, the ITA's ITC Recapture regime ensures that SR&ED tax credits are retained solely on the net cost of property consumed in R&D rather than subsidizing commercial production assets. Recapture is triggered whenever property whose cost was previously claimed as a qualified SR&ED expenditure—specifically transformed materials, commercial conversions, or depreciable capital property acquired either before 2014 or after December 15, 2024—is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use. In the taxation year of disposition or commercial conversion, the recaptured ITC amount is added directly to the taxpayer's federal income tax payable and reported on T2 Schedule 31 (T2SCH31) for corporations or Form T2038-IND for individuals.
3. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures and Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method Election

Every SR&ED claimant must choose annually on Form T661 between two overhead calculation regimes: electing the Proxy Method on Line 160 or choosing the Traditional Method on Line 162. Under the Proxy Method (governed by ITA clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) and ITR subsections 2900(4), 2900(6), and 2900(9)), the claimant excludes all actual SR&ED overhead and indirect expenditures from Form T661 (deducting them instead as ordinary business expenses) and adds a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Line 502 when computing qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes. Following post-2013 transition rules on Line 820 of Part 5, Section B of Form T661, the PPA rate equals 55% of the eligible direct SR&ED salary base.

Under the Traditional Method (ITA clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)), no notional PPA is added; instead, the claimant itemizes and substantiates actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 that are "directly attributable" (direct and incremental) to performing SR&ED in Canada. Beyond overhead mechanics, this election alters eligible salary categories and post-2024 equipment lease deductibility.

body.text: 3.2 Salary or Wages, Specified Employees, and Foreign SR&ED Labour

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, eligible SR&ED "salary or wages" represent employment income computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I (generally T4 gross wages paid or incurred in the year). For regular (non-specified) employees, claimable SR&ED wages include base pay, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, employment inducements or non-competition payments treated as employment remuneration (though inducements are excluded from the PPA salary base), cash outlays for taxable benefits, and reasonable estimates of actual costs for non-cash taxable benefits—such as automobile benefits, housing/board/meals, group term life insurance, gifts/awards, interest-free/low-interest loans, and tuition—provided recoverable GST/HST or PST is excluded and the underlying cost is not double-claimed as a business expense. Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages never include the employer's share of payroll benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, or pension contributions), extended vacation or sick leave, stock option benefits, or retiring allowances. Under the Proxy Method (ITA subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV)), only employees "directly engaged" in hands-on SR&ED, commensurate direct support, or direct technical supervision qualify (excluding non-technological management and clerical staff); if an employee spends all or substantially all of their employment time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary is included. When calculating the 55% PPA salary base, however, ITR subsection 2900(9) excludes all bonuses and profit-based remuneration for all employees.

Stringent statutory restrictions govern "specified employees"—defined under subsection 248(1) and section 251 of the ITA as any employee who is a specified shareholder owning (directly, indirectly, or together with non-arm's-length persons) 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, sibling, or child of a controlling shareholder). First, under subsection 37(9), bonuses and remuneration based on profits for specified employees are 100% disallowed. Second, under subsection 37(9.1) (and clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B)), a specified employee's claimable SR&ED salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days in the year the individual was a specified employee. Third, under subsections 37(9.2) through 37(9.5), where a specified employee works for two or more associated corporations, the group must allocate that single 5 × YMPE cap on Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) and file Form T1174 on or before each corporation's SR&ED reporting deadline; otherwise, the specified employee's SR&ED salary is statutorily deemed not to be an SR&ED expenditure (nil). Fourth, under ITR subsection 2900(6), a specified employee's inclusion in the 55% PPA salary base is separately capped using a 2.5 × YMPE limit (allocated across associated corporations or partnerships where applicable).

For SR&ED work performed outside Canada, subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA allows a claimant to include permissible foreign SR&ED salaries—allocated on Form T661 between Line 307 (non-specified employees) and Line 309 (specified employees)—equal to the lesser of Amount A or Amount B. Amount A comprises actual foreign SR&ED salaries meeting five cumulative conditions: (1) directly undertaken by the claimant's own employee (never a contractor); (2) the employee was a resident of Canada when the expense was incurred; (3) the work related to a business of the claimant; (4) the work was an integral part and solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada (disqualifying dual-purpose activities supporting foreign R&D or non-SR&ED work); and (5) the salary was not subject to foreign income or profits tax. Amount B caps total foreign SR&ED wages at 10% of total domestic SR&ED salaries claimed on Line 306 of Form T661 (meaning Maximum Line 309 = (10% × Line 306) − Line 307). In CRA's policy example, if five Canadian-resident engineers earn $9,000/month ($540,000 total) and one works outside Canada for five months solely supporting Canadian SR&ED without foreign tax, Amount A is $45,000 ($9,000 × 5) and domestic Line 306 salary is $495,000 ($540,000 − $45,000), yielding an Amount B cap of $49,500 (10% × $495,000); because $45,000 is less than $49,500, the full $45,000 qualifies on Line 307.
3.3 Reinstated Capital Expenditures, Depreciation (CCA), Shared-Use Equipment, Leases, and Cloud/Software Costs

Following Bill C-15 and CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8 and October 2026), capital assets are governed by a strict acquisition-date boundary: depreciable property acquired on or before December 15, 2024 (including property deemed made before December 16, 2024 under available-for-use rules) is ineligible, whereas property acquired after December 15, 2024 (and lease amounts first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024) qualifies.

Full SR&ED capital expenditures (claimed on Line 390 and included in total allowable SR&ED expenditures on Line 400) apply to new or used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 where the claimant intended at acquisition either to use the property all or substantially all (ASA)—90% or more—of its operating time over its expected useful life in SR&ED in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value in SR&ED in Canada. Capital cost encompasses purchase price, installation, customs and excise duties, transportation, and direct acquisition costs. Claimants must report on Line 262 and Line 263 of Form T661 the names and SR&ED operating-time percentages of up to the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties claimed on Line 390 per project.

Where new depreciable equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 is used primarily (more than 50%, but less than 90%) in SR&ED, it falls under the Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) regime rather than section 37 immediate expensing. Specifically, SUE capital cost does not enter the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and must instead be depreciated under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rates and rules on T2 Schedule 8 (T2SCH8). Under both the Proxy Method and Traditional Method, however, SUE earns SR&ED ITCs on Line 504 (and Box 792) of Form T661 on 25% of its capital cost in the first period (first-term SUE) and another 25% of its capital cost in the second period (second-term SUE). Similarly, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time can be claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures only when the claimant uses the Traditional Method.

Regarding cloud computing and software costs, auditors evaluate software, cloud infrastructure, and software-as-a-service (SaaS) outlays under the established statutory categories above: depreciable software/hardware property or right-to-use capital acquisitions made after December 15, 2024 must satisfy the post-December 15, 2024 capital or lease rules, while non-capital cloud compute or software subscriptions are excluded from Form T661 if the claimant elects the Proxy Method (being covered notionally by the 55% PPA on Line 502) and can only be claimed as actual SR&ED overhead on Line 360 if the claimant elects the Traditional Method and proves the expenses are directly attributable (incremental) to SR&ED.
3.4 Materials, Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transactions, and 180-Day Unpaid Amounts

Form T661 separates direct physical materials into materials consumed (Line 320) and materials transformed (Line 325). CRA's ITC policy confirms the critical downstream audit difference: transformed materials incorporated into prototypes or commercializable output remain subject to ITC recapture if subsequently sold or converted to commercial use.

For outsourced R&D, subsection 127(9) restricts arm's-length SR&ED contract expenditures performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf and third-party payments to 80% inclusion in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (implemented by deducting 20% on Form T661). Furthermore, contract payments earn 0% ITC if paid or payable to a person or partnership that is not a "taxable supplier" (cross-referenced to Section 9.0 of CRA's qualified expenditures policy). Where R&D is outsourced to a non-arm's-length (NAL) party, subsection 127(9) excludes the contract payment entirely from the payer's qualified expenditures. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED costs or jointly elects on Form T1146 to transfer qualified expenditures (limited for capital to property acquired after December 15, 2024) to the NAL payer on Line 540. Similarly, under subsections 127(11.5) and 127(11.6), purchases of non-contract goods or services from an NAL supplier are capped for ITC purposes at the actual cost to the NAL supplier of providing those goods or services (adjusted on Lines 542 and 543), stripping out intercompany markups.

Finally, accrued year-end SR&ED liabilities face two strict 180-day cash payment cutoffs. Under ITA subsection 78(4), employee remuneration unpaid within 180 days after taxation year-end is deemed not incurred in that year for SR&ED expenditure pool purposes. Under ITA subsection 127(26), current SR&ED expenditures other than salary or wages (such as contractor invoices or materials) unpaid within 180 days after taxation year-end are excluded from that year's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (for arm's-length contracts, 80% of the unpaid balance is removed, and when actually paid in a later taxation year, 80% of the paid amount is added back on Form T661 for that subsequent year).
4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Ten of Canada's thirteen provinces and territories supplement federal SR&ED incentives with regional R&D tax credits; Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut offer no provincial or territorial R&D tax credits. Outside Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered provincially under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act), all participating provincial and territorial R&D credits harmonize with federal SR&ED definitions and are administered directly by the CRA.
4.1 Québec's 2025–2026 Innovation Tax Overhaul: CRIC and IDCI

In Québec Budget 2025–2026 (tabled March 25, 2025), the Gouvernement du Québec abolished eight legacy innovation tax measures—including its former R&D salary and partnership credits as well as the refundable tax credit for technological adaptation services—for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with a streamlined two-pillar framework comprising the CRIC and the IDCI.

Effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 (with an estimated 2026 provincial tax expenditure of $673.1 million), the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D, l'innovation et la précommercialisation, claimed by attaching Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T to the Québec corporate income tax return) provides a 100% refundable credit to any eligible corporation operating a business with an establishment in Québec, regardless of size or foreign control. CRIC pays 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above an annual exclusion threshold and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 tier. Crucially, CRIC expands beyond core R&D (basic research, applied research, and experimental development) to cover eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with R&D—specifically: (a) tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for initial commercialization approval or certification; and (b) product design, encompassing form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and material selection.

Qualified CRIC expenditures encompass 100% of wages paid to Québec-establishment employees, NAL Québec subcontractor payments reasonably attributable to Québec employee wages, 50% of arm's-length Québec subcontractor payments, 50% of payments to eligible Québec public research centres, research consortia, or university entities, and 100% of eligible capital property acquisition costs in Québec—excluding land, buildings, rights to use land or buildings, and property covered by a Large Investment Project tax holiday. Qualified expenditures must exceed an annual applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum across all eligible R&D and pre-commercialization employees of the Québec Basic Personal Amount under section 752.0.0.1 of the Taxation Act ($18,571 for 2025, indexed automatically each year), adjusted in proportion to each employee's time devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization work. For example, if a Québec corporation (tax year starting April 1, 2025) incurs $440,000 in 100%-dedicated R&D salaries across four employees, $200,000 in arm's-length Québec subcontracting (50% = $100,000 eligible), and $150,000 in lab equipment ($690,000 total qualified expenditures), its exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 or 4 × $18,571 = $74,284, leaving $615,716 in net excess expenditures and yielding a 100% refundable CRIC of $184,714.80 (30% × $615,716).

Complementing front-end CRIC refunds, Québec's Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations in Québec (IDCI / DICI) (projected at $64.8 million in 2026 tax relief) grants corporations with a Québec establishment a taxable income deduction yielding an effective Québec corporate tax rate of 2% on eligible income derived from commercializing qualified intellectual property assets (APIA).
4.2 Ontario, Western Canada, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

In Ontario, corporations carrying on SR&ED through an Ontario permanent establishment under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) can stack up to three CRA-administered credits (alongside transitional schedules T2SCH506 and T2SCH507). The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) provides an 8% fully refundable credit up to a $3,000,000 annual expenditure cap (maximum $240,000 cash refund, claimed on T2SCH566 together with T2SCH31), phasing out where prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or prior-year taxable paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) (sections 38 to 45, claimed on T2SCH508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit with no expenditure cap, carrying back 3 years (not prior to January 1, 2009) and forward 20 years. In addition, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) delivers a 20% fully refundable credit on qualified R&D contracts with eligible Ontario research institutes up to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap per associated group (claimed on T2SCH568 and T2SCH569).

Across Western Canada, British Columbia (Income Tax Act (BC), sections 97 to 103) provides a 10% SR&ED credit claimed on Form T666 within 18 months of tax year-end: 100% refundable for CCPCs and ECPCs up to a $6,000,000 expenditure limit ($600,000 max refund) for tax years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (previously $3,000,000 for CCPCs, with a $300,000 max refund) and 10% non-refundable (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward) above the expenditure limit or for other corporations. The Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026 (S.B.C. 2026, c. 5) made the BC credit permanent and, for tax years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, extended the refundable credit to ECPCs, raised the expenditure limit to $6,000,000 (phased out for CCPCs between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital), and restored capital expenditures as BC qualified expenditures. Alberta independently administers its Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (Alberta Corporate Tax Act, sections 26.95 to 26.99; Information Circular IEG-1), a 100% refundable grant on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta SR&ED-aligned spending paying 8% up to the corporation's two-year average Alberta R&D base spending and 20% on incremental spending above that two-year base, claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 and AT4970 within 15 months after the filing-due date. Saskatchewan (The Income Tax Act (SK), sections 63 to 63.4, T2SCH403) provides CCPCs a 10% refundable credit up to a $1,000,000 annual cap and a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward) on CCPC spending above $1,000,000 and for all non-CCPCs. Manitoba (Income Tax Act (MB), section 7.3, T2SCH380, filed within 1 year after the filing-due date) provides a 15% credit: for in-house R&D, half (7.5%) is refundable and 7.5% is non-refundable (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward), whereas R&D contracted to a qualifying Manitoba institute is 100% refundable (15%) and contracts with eligible Manitoba educational institutions are exempted from the federal 80% reduction.

In Atlantic Canada and the North, New Brunswick (section 59, T2SCH360), Nova Scotia (section 41, T2SCH340, filed within 18 months after tax year-end), and Newfoundland and Labrador (section 42, T2SCH301 for corporations and T1129 for individuals, filed within 12 months after the filing-due date) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit (with historical non-refundable New Brunswick credits carrying back 3 years and forward 7 years, and no expenditure caps). Yukon offers a CRA-administered 15% fully refundable R&D credit plus an additional 5% refundable credit (totalling 20%) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University (claimed on T2SCH442 for corporations or Form T1232 for individuals within 12 months after the filing-due date under section 15 of the Income Tax Act (Yukon), with no expenditure cap).

body.text: 5. Direct Federal Innovation Grants and Government Assistance Grinding Mechanics
5.1 NRC IRAP (Including 2026 DI Assist) and ISED Strategic Innovation Fund

Established in 1947 and operating as one of Canada's four flagship innovation platforms alongside the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), the Canadian Trade Commissioner Service, and Regional Development Agencies, the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) delivers non-repayable R&D contributions and technical advisory services to incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs (500 or fewer FTEs) through more than 250 field staff—including Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs)—across 130 offices in five regional directorates (with ICT/digital economy firms representing 29% of clients). Unlike entitlement-based SR&ED tax credits, NRC IRAP requires upfront ITA evaluation and an approved contribution agreement before project costs are incurred, reimbursing monthly claims for a portion of direct technical salaries (excluding benefits and overhead) and approved contractor costs. Alongside core R&D project funding, the Youth Employment Program (6-to-12-month placements of minimum 30 hours/week for Canadian post-secondary graduates aged 15 to 30), and IP Assist (up to Level 3 funding to execute IP strategies), the federal government launched Defence Industry Assist (DI Assist) in January 2026 with over $240 million through NRC IRAP to help Canadian SMEs develop and commercialize sovereign defence and dual-use technologies supporting Canada's Defence Industrial Strategy and 2% NATO target. For larger-scale R&D, facility expansion, and mandate attraction projects, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) administers the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), offering repayable, partially non-repayable, and fully non-repayable contributions across Business Innovation and Growth and Collaborations and Networks streams.
5.2 Statutory "Government Assistance" Stacking and Grinding Calculation

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment in respect of SR&ED that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its tax return filing-due date reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (and reduces the deductible section 37 expenditure pool), whereas subsequent repayments of government assistance generate ITCs in the year repaid. Both non-repayable grants (such as NRC IRAP) and provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool (note that under Alberta's statute, the Alberta IEG and federal SR&ED ITC do not grind the Alberta IEG base, though the Alberta credit still grinds the federal pool). Because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the Proxy Method is added to allowable SR&ED salaries before subtracting government assistance in Part 4 of Form T661, stacking an NRC IRAP grant with provincial and federal SR&ED credits preserves the full 55% PPA uplift on gross SR&ED payroll, as shown in the following step-by-step Manitoba CCPC audit model:

items: Direct Non-Specified SR&ED Salaries (Form T661, Line 380 / Line 400): Suppose a qualifying CCPC with a permanent establishment in Manitoba incurs $1,000,000 in direct in-house SR&ED salaries in its 2026 taxation year, elects the Proxy Method, and receives a $200,000 NRC IRAP salary grant.
Add Notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 502): 55% × $1,000,000 = $550,000, producing a pre-assistance expenditure and PPA total of $1,550,000.

Subtract NRC IRAP Government Assistance: $1,550,000 − $200,000 = $1,350,000 net eligible expenditure base for Manitoba R&D tax credit purposes (since Manitoba adopts federal ITC-eligible expenditures reduced by government assistance).

Compute Manitoba 15% R&D Tax Credit (T2SCH380): 15% × $1,350,000 = $202,500 total Manitoba credit, comprising $101,250 in cash refund (7.5%) and $101,250 in non-refundable Manitoba tax credit (7.5%, 20-year carryforward).
Subtract Manitoba Credit to Determine Federal Qualified Pool: $1,350,000 − $202,500 = $1,147,500 federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool.
Compute Federal 35% Enhanced Refundable ITC (T2SCH31): 35% × $1,147,500 = $401,625 federal cash refund.

Combined Incentive Recovery: The corporation recovers $702,875 in immediate cash ($200,000 IRAP + $101,250 Manitoba cash + $401,625 federal cash, or 70.29% of payroll) plus $101,250 in Manitoba tax credits, totalling $804,125 (80.41% of payroll)—up from $693,625 total ($577,375 cash) without NRC IRAP.

body.text: 6. Governing Authorities, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval, Tax Forms, and Statutory Deadlines
6.1 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and CRA Administration

While the Department of Finance Canada writes SR&ED tax legislation, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers federal and harmonized provincial SR&ED claims through technical reviews conducted by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) alongside financial claim reviews (with small businesses accounting for 65% of all SR&ED claims submitted in the 2025–2026 fiscal year). On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process, enabling eligible businesses to apply via My Business Account before starting SR&ED work or incurring project costs to receive an upfront project eligibility determination within eight weeks. Claimants can request individual pre-application guidance (OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca), and CRA updated The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants in 2026 alongside late-fall 2026 upgrades to the SR&ED Client Portal and Self-Assessment and Learning Tool. Securing pre-claim approval does not waive post-year-end filing: claimants must still file a timely Form T661, indicating pre-claim approval on Line 212 and entering the pre-claim approval case number on Line 214.
6.2 Updated May 2026 Tax Forms, Strict 18-Month Deadlines, and Part 9 Penalties

In May 2026, the CRA issued updated SR&ED forms reflecting Bill C-15's enactment, adding a mandatory 5-digit Field of Research (FOR) code under the Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0 on Line 207 of Form T661, pre-claim approval fields on Lines 212 and 214, top-10 depreciable property disclosures on Lines 262 and 263, and post-December 15, 2024 capital restrictions on Lines 518, 532, 535, and 540.

body.text: A claimant's statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 12 months after the income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year. Because corporate T2 returns are due 6 months after year-end, corporations have exactly 18 months from the end of the taxation year to file Form T661 (and Schedule 31 / Form T1174); individuals have 17.5 months from the end of the tax year; and partnerships must file Form T661 with the partnership information return no later than 12 months after the earliest of all member filing-due dates for the tax year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends (noting also that Budget 2026 proposes shifting individual T1 filing and balance-due dates to May 15 starting in the 2027 taxation year). Enforcement is absolute: any expenditure not reported on Form T661 by the statutory reporting deadline is permanently barred from SR&ED tax incentives. Furthermore, Part 9 of Form T661 mandates full disclosure of any external claim preparer—name (Line 940), Business Number (Line 945), billing arrangement code (Line 950), billing rate (Line 955), other arrangements up to 10 words (Line 960), and total fee paid or expected (Line 965), or certification on Lines 935, 970, and 975 that no preparer assisted—backed by statutory claim preparer penalties under ITA subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3). Budget 2026 separately proposes increasing most fixed-dollar ITA penalties to account for inflation, for taxation years ending after 2027, and indexing them to inflation once every five years.
7. Judicial Precedents, Technical Eligibility, and CRA Audit Defence
7.1 Subsection 248(1) Scope and the Five Northwest Hydraulic Judicial Questions

To qualify under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, claimed work must constitute basic research (advancing scientific knowledge without a practical application in view), applied research (advancing scientific knowledge with a practical application in view), or experimental development (achieving technological advancement to create new, or incrementally improve existing, materials, devices, products, or processes), together with commensurate support work directly supporting those core activities under paragraph (d), while excluding social science research, routine quality control testing, commercial production, and market research.

Canadian courts evaluate subsection 248(1) eligibility using the foundational five-question test articulated by Justice Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC), adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. and applied across subsequent Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal jurisprudence—including Jentel Manufacturing (June 11, 2010 TCC), Joel Theatrical Rigging (January 2017 TCC), National R&D Inc. (July 7, 2020 TCC), and recent appellate rulings (2021 FCA 88; 2022 FCA 72)—requiring an affirmative ("yes") answer to all five criteria:

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures accessible to competent professionals in the field?
Hypothesis Formulation: Did the person claiming to perform SR&ED formulate specific hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?

Scientific Method Discipline: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the systematic formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through experiment or analysis?

Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement—an advancement in general scientific or technological understanding (including conclusive knowledge gained from failed experiments)?
Contemporaneous Records: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: In Tax Court litigation, under the Supreme Court of Canada's burden-of-proof rule in Hickman Motors Ltd., a claimant must adduce credible prima facie evidence demolishing the Minister's assessment assumptions—a standard routinely lost (as in Jentel Manufacturing) when taxpayers lack contemporaneous experimental records demonstrating systematic investigation.
7.2 CRA's "Why" and "How" Review Framework and Audit-Defence Protocol

In its administrative guidance and Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, the CRA distils subsection 248(1) and the five Northwest Hydraulic questions into two operational pillars without altering the underlying statutory test: the "Why" (demonstrating why the work was undertaken to overcome a scientific or technological uncertainty and achieve a technological advancement beyond standard practice) and the "How" (demonstrating how a systematic investigation progressed from a defined baseline through hypothesis formulation, testing, and analysis). To safeguard post-2024 claims against technical or financial disallowance, claimants should execute five operational controls:

items: Evaluate Pre-Claim Approval Before Project Launch: Submit proposed R&D projects through My Business Account under the Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process launched April 1, 2026 to obtain an eight-week CRA eligibility ruling prior to committing capital, recording the resulting case number on Lines 212 and 214 of Form T661.

Capture Contemporaneous Experimental Evidence: Maintain dated hypotheses, test matrices, failure logs, analytical models, and source-control repositories generated as the work progresses rather than relying on year-end retrospective summaries.

Maintain Granular Payroll and Capital Operating Logs: Track employee hours by SR&ED project to substantiate "directly engaged" status under the Proxy Method, and log operating-time percentages for every post-December 15, 2024 depreciable asset to substantiate the ≥90% ASA threshold on Lines 262, 263, and 390 (or primary use for Line 504 Shared-Use Equipment).

Enforce 150-Day Post-Year-End Payment Sweeps: Settle all accrued SR&ED wages, bonuses, contractor invoices, and material payables well ahead of the strict 180-day statutory cutoff under subsections 78(4) and 127(26).

Audit Group Allocations and Filing Deadlines: Model whether associated CCPCs benefit from electing into the ECPC three-year revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million), verify Part 9 preparer fee disclosures under subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3), and file Form T661, Schedule 31, Schedule 49, Form T1174, Form T1145, Form T1146, and provincial schedules strictly ahead of the non-extendable 18-month corporate (or earlier provincial) deadline.
